who-this-is-for.text: A reviewer deciding whether the model is the right model. The build already answers whether these are proved — all forty-two are, from the standard axioms and nothing else. It cannot answer whether they say what the interface promised, and that is the question this page exists to make answerable.

what-is-bound.text: Six artifacts, each with its hash: the model, its lemmas, the statements, the audit module, the corpus generator and the corpus itself. Every one ships beside the page, and a mirror check fails if the shipped copy and the built copy differ in either direction. Changing any bound input invalidates this record.

the-shape-the-promises-are-made-over.text: Almost every promise is stated over reachable states — genesis, closed under accepted folds — and not over arbitrary values of the state type. This is not a weakening dressed up as a hypothesis: over an arbitrary state value the supply laws are false, because nothing stops you writing down a state with three active tokens for one key. Reachability is what makes them true, and it is exactly the property a chain enforces by only ever arriving at a state through a fold.

Where a promise does not need reachability, it does not assume it. The seven inversions, the empty-batch refusal, the fold equation and the read-changes-nothing statement hold over any state at all, because they are statements about what an accepted edge did rather than about what the ledger holds.

reading-the-promises-back.text: No tree change without approval. If a request is accepted and it is not the read, an approval was present, minted under the registry's own pinned policy, and its asset name is the hash of the edge, the key, the owner and the destination of this request. A correct policy is necessary and not sufficient: an approval for a different key, under the very same policy, does not admit the request.

Soundness says a terminal attestation exists only for a leaf that really is terminal, and its companion supplies the provenance half — the only edge that can bring a terminal token into existence is the read. Permanence says what that attestation claims stays true through any later sequence of folds, which is what lets a holder keep the witness rather than re-reading the chain.

The supply law is a biconditional over every key: the count of outstanding active tokens is one exactly when the leaf is active, and zero otherwise. Occupancy comes with its converse, which matters as much as the rule, because a registry that refused everything would satisfy the rule perfectly. Termination says that on a terminal key every leaf-moving edge is refused — the refusal is the complement of the edge table, so there is no unlisted case that quietly moves a retired name.

Of the four witness laws, the third is the one to read closely: terminal attestations are plural. Any number may exist, each is true, and minting another changes nothing — which is the consequence of the attestation being a read. And the two edges that consume an absent witness pay the deposit back to the refund address the original request named, not to the output of the consuming request and not to whoever folded it.

what-the-model-does-not-say.text: These are limits of the model, not gaps in the proofs. Keys and owners are integers. Approvals carry a policy and a tuple; no signature is checked. The deposit is a number that must arrive at a named address, not lovelace. Retirement is certified by the recovery commitment or a distinct-member quorum and never by the control key alone — the model says so, but it models no signature scheme.

The last row is the important one. Everything here is about a model. Whether the deployed validator implements it is a different question with a different kind of evidence behind it, and this page is not that evidence.

how-much-independence-this-record-has.text: Stated plainly, because a reader cannot see it from the outside: the model, the corpus generator, the simulator transcription and this readback all have the same author. A misunderstanding of the interface made while writing the model will be made again while transcribing it and again while reading it back, and none of the three will catch it. They are not independent measurements; they are one measurement repeated.

What the internal machinery does catch is real but narrower: transcription slips, statements that do not constrain what they appear to, unproved obligations, and drift between the shipped Lean and the built Lean. The check this record cannot perform on itself is the one that matters most — whether the statements say what the interface promised. That requires someone who did not write them.
